title.en: Tissues: hands-on activities from the textbook

text.en: Why does a cut onion root stop growing, why does a cut ooze blood, and why can your elbow bend but your skull cannot? Chapter 3 answers with simple activities.

Activity 3.1 designs an experiment with two onion bulbs in jars of water. Measure the roots on days 1, 2 and 3.
On day 3, cut about 1 cm off the root tips of the bulb in Jar B and measure both again for four more days.
The roots with cut tips stop growing while the others continue. Growth is concentrated at the root tip, which has dividing meristematic tissue.
Activity 3.2 links everyday experience to tissue. A small cut oozes red blood and then a clot forms, so blood is a tissue that carries substances and seals wounds.
Activity 3.3 identifies connective tissues by action. Touching your elbow feels hard and rigid and gives strength and support, which is bone tissue.
Activity 3.4 asks what fraction of body weight comes from bones and muscles. On average adult males have about 40 to 50 per cent muscle and females about 30 to 40 per cent, while bone is about 12 to 15 per cent for all adults.
Activity 3.5 asks you to move body parts and record what each can do: complete rotation, partial rotation, or only bending. Joints decide the kind of movement.
Together the activities show that tissues are groups of similar cells doing a particular job.

problem.en: A student weighs 50 kg. Using the textbook average of 40 per cent muscle for an adult male, estimate muscle mass. (Illustration only.)

text.en: Muscle share = 40 per cent of body weight.
Muscle mass is about 20 kg for this illustration.

prompt.en: What does the onion root experiment show and how?

requiredIdeas.en: Growth is at the root tip

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking all parts of a root grow equally

points.en: Root growth is at the tip where dividing tissue is found.
Blood forms a clot to seal a cut.
Bone gives rigid support; muscles and joints allow movement.
Adult bone is about 12 to 15 per cent of body weight.
